problem: Existing social robot navigation (SRN) and human motion prediction datasets mostly contain sparse, distant interactions, lack autonomous robot deployments or controlled conditions, and rarely record user impressions, multiple robot platforms or multiple cultural sites.
motivation: HMP and SRN models trained on data only work if the training distribution matches deployment, and robots in constrained indoor spaces face close, fast encounters. Perceived social competence depends on robot embodiment and culture, so data should vary these factors and record human impressions.
key_idea: Collect a controlled lab dataset of close two-human plus one-robot encounters, using five HMP-based MPC navigation controllers on two robot platforms at two sites (USA, France), with motion capture, video and user survey impressions.
insight: Motion metrics alone do not separate controllers: CV, CoHAN and HST look similar in robot motion statistics but received very different user impressions, so subjective ratings are needed to identify desirable SRN behavior. Comparisons against other datasets show Bi3 has the lowest minimum human-human distance at both sites and the highest velocity at LAAS, so it is harder for HMP. Site differences (larger PR2 vs. Stretch, and culture) are confounded and cannot be separated.
method: Scenario design: two participants assemble block towers between perimeter workstations in a 3.5x3.5 m space, with ordering designed to force path crossings; the robot follows a random workstation sequence, mirrored each trial
MPC social navigation system: receding-horizon MPPI control (2000 samples, max speed 0.3 m/s, differential drive) with cost = goal distance + personal-space violation + workspace boundary

Five HMP models embedded in MPC: No Prediction, Static, Constant Velocity, Human Scene Transformer (trained on ETH/UCY ZARA1, 20 modes, most likely used), CoHAN (joint cooperative planning); h=8 history, T=12 horizon, 0.4 s step
Data collection protocol: 37 experiments (17 UM Stretch, 20 LAAS PR2), 74 subjects, 5 trials each, balanced Latin square ordering, surveys after each trial

Recorded data: 120 Hz OptiTrack motion capture, top-down RGB video 30 Hz, Stretch egocentric RealSense depth 15 Hz, ROS bags, per-cycle HMP predictions/goals/velocity commands in JSON, workspace/goal annotations
User impressions: RoSAS (Discomfort and Competence, 9-point) and NASA TLX (21-point), plus open-ended comments (285 survey responses, 78 comments from 57 participants)

setting.backbone: MPPI-based MPC with five HMP models (NP, ST, CV, HST transformer pretrained on ETH/UCY ZARA1, CoHAN)
setting.training_data: Dataset paper; HST checkpoint pretrained on ZARA1 of ETH/UCY; other models need no training
setting.observation: Overhead OptiTrack mocap for perfect human and robot states; top-down RGB video; egocentric RGB-D on Stretch (UM only)
setting.action_space: continuous linear and angular velocity for a differential-drive robot
setting.privileged: Robot assumed to perfectly observe human states via motion capture; known workspace boundary and goals

numbers_note: Dataset paper; no navigation success benchmarks. Only descriptive statistics (RoSAS/TLX tables, motion statistic figures) are reported.
results: Bi3 contains 10.5 hours of data, 37 experiments and 74 participants across two sites. Analysis shows lower minimum human distance than other datasets, high and diverse human velocity, and strongly different user impressions across controllers and sites, with HST getting the most positive comments and NP and CoHAN the most negative.
limitations: Robot platform and culture/site are confounded, so effects cannot be attributed to either
Robot speed capped at 0.3 m/s, mocap-based perfect perception, and a single structured lab task in a small workspace
Some UM participants opted out of survey release, and only 2 humans plus one robot are covered; no benchmark model training results are given
